Introduction

The Story of the King's Foolish Sons

In the southern country, there was a city called Maidens' Delight. King Immortal-Power lived there with his three sons, Rich-Power, Fierce-Power, and Endless-Power. However, these princes were complete blockheads.

The king noticed that his sons had no interest in learning. He called his advisors and said, "These sons of mine are not interested in education. They lack common sense. When I see them, my kingdom doesn't bring me happiness, no matter how many external problems I solve."

The advisors suggested different methods to educate the princes, but one advisor, Keen, had a clever idea. He said, "Your Majesty, we can't teach them in a short time. They need to learn the basics of grammar, then move on to books on religion and practical life. It will take twelve years."

But Keen had another idea. He said, "Since life is short, and verbal sciences take a long time to master, let's create a summary of the essential facts. This way, we can make them intelligent in a short time."

The king liked Keen's idea and decided to find someone who could create this summary. He was introduced to a wise Brahman named Vishnusharman, who was known for his knowledge in many subjects.

Vishnusharman was asked to make the princes intelligent in six months' time. If he succeeded, the king would give him a hundred land-grants. But if he failed, he would have to give up his own name.

Vishnusharman agreed to take on the task. He said, "I'm not interested in money, and I'm not afraid of you, King. I'm eighty years old, and I've lost interest in worldly pleasures. But I'll show you my skills. If I fail, I'll give up my name."

The king was amazed by Vishnusharman's bold promise and entrusted the princes to him. Meanwhile, Vishnusharman took the princes home and made them learn five books he had written: "The Loss of Friends," "The Winning of Friends," "Crows and Owls," "Loss of Gains," and "Ill-considered Action."

The princes learned the books, and in six months' time, they became intelligent and knowledgeable. From that day on, the Panchatantra, or the "Five Books," traveled the world, teaching people how to live wisely.

Moral: The right guidance at the right time can change the course of a person's life and help them become intelligent and wise.

The Loss of Friends

In the city of Maidens' Delight, a merchant named Increase lived a life of virtue and wealth. He pondered one night and came to a conclusion: "Wealth, if not increased, will dwindle like soot. Even a small amount, if added to, will grow like an anthill. Therefore, wealth should be earned, guarded, and increased."

Increase collected merchandise for the city of Mathura and set out with his servants. He had two strong bulls, Joyful and Lively, to carry the load. As they traveled, Lively became exhausted and sank in the mud. The driver reported to Increase that Lively had died.

Increase was sad for a moment but continued his journey to Mathura. He left caretakers with Lively's food and said, "If he lives, bring him to me; if he dies, perform the last rites." The men, fearing the forest's dangers, made a false report that Lively had died.

In reality, Lively survived and hobbled to the bank of the Jumna River, where he regained his strength and became plump and energetic. He spent his days browsing on grass blades and tearing ant hills with his horns.

One day, a lion named Rusty came to the Jumna River with his retinue. He heard Lively's loud bellow and felt uneasy but hid his feelings. He gathered his company, including his two jackal friends, Cheek and Victor, under a banyan tree.

Rusty was a proud and powerful lion who relied on his strength and courage. He had no need for fancy trappings or education but ruled his kingdom with pride and heroism. His subjects looked up to him as their king.

Lively and Rusty soon became friends. They talked together every day. Lively was wise and taught the lion many things. Rusty took such delight in Lively that he began to neglect his own court.

Cheek and Victor, the two jackals, watched with worry. They had lost their place and their favor with the king. Victor said, "Let us separate them and win back the king." Cheek warned, "Meddling brings nothing but trouble." But Victor went to Rusty and told a lie. He said, "Lively plans to kill you and seize your throne." Then he went to Lively and told another lie. He said, "Rusty means to kill you." So the two friends grew suspicious and afraid of each other. They met in the forest and fought. Rusty killed Lively. When his anger had passed, Rusty looked at his dead friend and wept. He said, "Lively was my second life. In killing him, I have only hurt myself."

Moral: Greed and malice can lead to the loss of true friends.

The Jackal and the War-Drum

There was a hungry jackal one day.

He wandered into a forest searching for food.

He came to a king's battle ground and heard a big sound.

The jackal felt sad and worried. "What's happening?" he thought.

He looked around and saw a big war-drum.

The drum was making a loud noise. "Who made this sound?" the jackal wondered.

He saw that the drum was quiet when the wind blew.

The jackal crept closer and saw that the drum was made of wood and leather.

He thought, "This drum must be full of meat and fat!"

The jackal was excited and decided to take a closer look.

He gnawed a hole in the drum and crawled inside.

But when he looked around, he was very disappointed.

He saw only wood and skin inside the drum.

The jackal laughed and said, "I was so silly! I thought it was full of food!"

Moral: Don't judge something by its noise or appearance.

Merchant Strong-Tooth

In the city of Growing City, a wise merchant named Strong-Tooth managed the administration. He was known for his cleverness and fairness. People loved him, and the king trusted him completely.

Strong-Tooth once had a daughter get married, and he invited the whole town and the king's entourage. He treated them with great honor, fed them, and gave them gifts. After the wedding, he escorted the king home, showing him great respect.

Bull, the king's lowly servant, was jealous of Strong-Tooth's position. He thought, "Why should I be angry? I won't hurt him. I'll just wait for the right moment." One morning, Bull saw Strong-Tooth near the king's bed and accused him of kissing the queen. The king believed Bull and withdrew his favor from Strong-Tooth.

Strong-Tooth was puzzled. He thought, "I've never done anything wrong. Why is the king angry with me?" He realized that Bull was behind the king's decision. Strong-Tooth reflected, "A lowly servant at the palace can still have honor and respect."

Strong-Tooth decided to clear his name. He summoned Bull and gave him two garments as a gift, explaining that he had driven him out because of his misbehavior. Bull was overjoyed and apologized for his actions.

The next day, Bull entered the palace and made another false accusation against the king. The king realized his mistake and reinstated Strong-Tooth, presenting him with gems and garments.

Moral: A little thing can lift someone high, and a little thing can bring them down.

Godly and June

There was a holy man named Godly.

He lived in a monastery with many treasures.

People gave him money for his sacrifices.

Godly trusted no one with his treasure.

He kept it under his arm always.

A rogue named June saw the treasure.

June thought, "How can I take this treasure?"

He couldn't break the stone wall.

He couldn't enter the door, it was too high.

June decided to befriend Godly.

He went to Godly and said, "Glory to Shiva."

June fell at Godly's feet and said, "I am a foolish man."

Godly was happy to have a new friend.

June said, "I am worried about the future."

Godly said, "You are wise to think about this."

Godly gave June advice on how to live.

He said, "You can change your life with prayer."

June was impressed and asked for a vow.

Godly agreed, but said June must sleep outside.

June was happy to take the vow.

Godly gave June initiation and made him a disciple.

June served Godly, but still kept an eye on the treasure.

June thought of killing Godly to get the treasure.

But then a pupil of Godly's came with an invitation.

Godly and June went to the ceremony.

At the river, Godly gave June his robe to watch.

June took the treasure and ran away.

Moral: Trusting no one can lead to trouble.

Godly and June

In a secluded monastery, a holy man named Godly lived. He had acquired a large sum of money by selling finely woven garments to the faithful. Godly trusted no one and kept his treasure close to him always.

A rogue named June, who stole money from others, observed Godly's treasure and thought: "How can I take this from him?" June couldn't break through the solid stone walls or enter the high door. He decided to win Godly's trust and become his disciple.

June approached Godly, bowed down, and said: "Glory to Shiva. Amen." He spoke with respect: "O holy sir, I see that life is short and fleeting. Delights are like a shadow. What should I do to safely cross the sea of life?" Godly was impressed by June's words.

Godly said: "You are blessed for being indifferent to the world at a young age. Saints are those who control their passions in youth. A holy sage's body may age, but their mind remains young." Godly then shared a prayer that could change one's caste and bring purity.

June listened and clasped Godly's feet. "Holy sir, please impose a vow on me." Godly agreed, but warned June not to enter his cell at night. June promised to follow the rules and take a vow.

As time passed, June served Godly, but still didn't trust him. He thought of killing Godly, but then a pupil's son arrived with an invitation for Godly to attend a ceremony. Godly took June along and, as they traveled, came to a river. He handed June his treasure and asked him to keep watch.

As soon as Godly was out of sight, June seized the treasure and ran away.

Leap and Creep

In a grand palace, a majestic bed stood, famous for its comfort and beauty. A plump and handsome louse named Creep lived on the bed's coverlet with her large family. She fed on the king's blood while he slept, growing stronger and healthier.

One day, a flea named Leap drifted in on the wind and landed on the bed. He was thrilled to see the luxurious coverlet, soft pillows, and sweet perfume. Leap was charmed by the bed's delightfulness and began to explore, eventually meeting Creep. She scolded him, "Where do you come from? This is a royal bed. Leave now and don't waste any more time."

Leap replied, "Madam, you shouldn't speak like that. As a guest, I deserve respect. I've tasted blood from various people, but this king's blood must be special. It's like nectar, free from impurities. I'd love to taste it and enjoy the pleasure and benefit."

Creep was taken aback by Leap's words. She remembered the story of a cunning prince who quoted a proverb to show respect to his guest. She agreed to let Leap stay, but with a condition: "You must not bite the king when he's drunk, tired, or asleep. That's the right time and place."

However, Leap misunderstood the condition and bit the king on the back when he was dozing off. The king was shocked and woke up, scratching his back and shouting for his servants to find the insect. Leap panicked and hid in a crevice, but the servants found Creep and her family, killing them instead.

The servants searched the bed, but Leap was nowhere to be found. They left, and the king was left with a painful scratch.

Moral: Being a good host means being mindful of your guests' needs and respecting their boundaries, lest you suffer the consequences.

Ugly's Trust Abused

In a distant city, a merchant named Ocean loaded a hundred camels with valuable cloth and set out on a journey. One of his camels, Ugly, was overburdened and fell limp, so Ocean divided the pack and left Ugly behind.

Days passed, and Ugly regained his strength by eating grass in the forest. A lion named Haughty, who lived in the forest with a leopard, a crow, and a jackal, came across Ugly. Haughty was impressed by Ugly's story and guaranteed his safety.

However, Haughty soon fell ill and couldn't hunt for food. His companions, the leopard, the crow, and the jackal, grew tired and hungry. They begged Haughty to let them find food for him, but he refused, saying he was on a diet.

The jackal and the crow started to plot against Ugly, suggesting that he be killed to feed Haughty. The jackal went to Haughty and proposed that Ugly be sacrificed, but Haughty was hesitant, remembering his promise to protect Ugly.

The jackal convinced Haughty that Ugly would volunteer to be killed if he knew it was for Haughty's sake. The other three animals then offered to sacrifice themselves, one by one, to feed Haughty. Each of them gave eloquent speeches, pleading with Haughty to accept their offer.

Ugly, however, thought that the others were using fancy words to avoid being eaten. He decided to make a speech of his own, hoping to outdo the others. Ugly bowed low and said, "Master, you can't eat any of them. Please take my life instead, so I can win the best of earth and heaven."

Haughty, moved by Ugly's words, gave the order, and the others tore Ugly's body apart. They devoured him, and Ugly finally gave up the ghost.

Moral: Those who live by their wits often end up being devoured by their own cleverness.

Shell-Neck, Slim, and Grim

There was a turtle named Shell-Neck.
He lived in a lake with friends Slim and Grim.
They were two ganders.

A big drought came to the land.
The lake dried up. Slim and Grim said, "Goodbye, Shell-Neck. We must leave."

Shell-Neck said, "Please don't go. I will die here. You can fly away, but I will drown."

Slim and Grim said, "We can't take you with us. You can't fly."

Shell-Neck said, "Bring a stick. I can grip it with my teeth. You can hold it with your bills and fly with me."

Slim and Grim said, "But if you talk, you will fall."

Shell-Neck said, "I promise to be quiet."

They flew over a city. People looked up and asked, "What are you carrying?"

Shell-Neck said, "What's all the noise about?"

He lost his grip and fell. People cut him up with knives.

Moral: Always listen carefully to good advice.

Smart, the Jackal

In a forest, a lion named Thunder-Fang lived with his advisors: Meat-Face the wolf, Smart the jackal, and Spike-Ear the camel. One day, Thunder-Fang fought a fierce elephant and was badly hurt. He ordered his famished friends to find food, but they couldn't find anything.

Smart thought, "If I can trick the lion into killing Spike-Ear, we'll have food for a few days." He approached Spike-Ear and said, "Friend, the lion is starving and if he leaves, we'll all starve too. I have a plan to save us both. If the lion kills you, we'll have food for a while, and he'll live longer too." Spike-Ear agreed, thinking it was a noble deed.

Smart proposed that Spike-Ear give his body to the lion at 100% interest, promising a double body in return. Spike-Ear agreed to this, but asked the Death-God to guarantee the bargain. The lion agreed, and Spike-Ear was killed.

When the lion went to the river to bathe, Smart said to Meat-Face, "You're starving, so eat the camel's heart before the lion returns." Meat-Face took a bite, but Smart shouted, "Drop it! The lion is coming!" When the lion returned, he saw the camel's heart was missing and was furious.

Meat-Face blamed Smart, but the lion realized he was innocent. Just then, a camel caravan was heard in the distance. The lion asked Smart to find out what the noise was. Smart pretended to investigate, then shouted, "Run, master! The Death-God is coming to punish you for killing Spike-Ear and eating the camel's heart!"

The lion fled, leaving Smart to eat the camel's body. Smart ate the meat slowly, making it last a long time.

Moral: Those who use their intelligence to harm others will eventually be punished for their selfish deeds.

Right-Mind and Wrong-Mind

Two friends, Right-Mind and Wrong-Mind, lived in a city.

They were sons of merchants and wanted to earn money.

They traveled to another country to make money.

Right-Mind found a pot with 1000 dinars.

He told Wrong-Mind, "We can go home now."

Wrong-Mind said, "Let's take 100 dinars each and bury the rest."

Right-Mind agreed. Each took 100 dinars.

They hid the rest in the ground and went home.

Wrong-Mind spent his 100 dinars quickly.

He asked Right-Mind to divide the rest.

Right-Mind said, "Let's take 200 dinars each."

Wrong-Mind took the rest and hid it.

A month later, Wrong-Mind went to Right-Mind.

He said, "Let's divide the rest equally."

They dug, but found nothing.

Wrong-Mind accused Right-Mind of stealing.

Right-Mind said, "I didn't steal it. I'm Right-Mind."

They took their dispute to court.

The magistrates decided to test them.

Wrong-Mind said, "I have a witness, the goddess of the wood."

The magistrates said, "Bring the goddess tomorrow."

Wrong-Mind went home and told his father.

He asked his father to be his witness.

His father said, "This is a bad plan. Think carefully."

The next day, they all went to the tree.

The magistrates asked, "Goddess, who took the money?"

A voice from the tree said, "Right-Mind took it."

Right-Mind said, "Please come out, goddess."

The voice did not come out.

So the magistrates looked inside the tree.

They found Wrong-Mind's father hiding there.

The trick was exposed.

Wrong-Mind had to give back the stolen money.

Right-Mind was free.

Moral: Think carefully before doing something.

The Mice That Ate Iron

In a certain town, a merchant named Naduk lived. He had lost his money and decided to travel abroad. A man who has lost his money cannot live in places where he once spent money like a rich man.

Naduk had an iron balance-beam in his house. It weighed a thousand pails and was passed down from his ancestors. He put it in pawn with Merchant Lakshman before he left for foreign lands.

After traveling for a long time, Naduk returned to his native city and asked Lakshman to return his balance-beam. But Lakshman said, "I'm sorry, Naduk, but the balance-beam has been eaten by mice."

Naduk said, "Lakshman, it's not your fault. Such is life. Nothing stays the same. I'm going to the river for a bath. Please send your son Money-God with me to carry my bathing things."

Lakshman was guilty and said, "My son, let's go with Uncle Naduk to the river." Money-God was happy to go with Naduk. After Naduk bathed, he pushed Money-God into a mountain cave and blocked the entrance with a big rock. Then he returned to Lakshman's house.

When Lakshman asked about his son, Naduk said, "A hawk carried him off from the river-bank." Lakshman was furious and said, "Naduk, you're lying! A hawk can't carry off a big boy like Money-God!"

Naduk replied, "But the mice ate a balance-beam made of iron. If you want your son back, give me the balance-beam." They took their dispute to the palace gate, and Lakshman cried out for help.

The magistrates said to Naduk, "Return Lakshman's son." Naduk said, "I'm telling the truth! A hawk carried him off." But the magistrates said, "You're not telling the truth. How can a hawk carry off a 15-year-old boy?"

Naduk laughed and said, "Gentlemen, listen to me. If mice can eat a balance-beam of iron, a hawk can steal an elephant. A boy is light as a feather."

The magistrates laughed and asked Naduk to explain. He told them the story of the balance-beam, and they laughed too. They ordered the balance-beam and Money-God to be returned to their rightful owners.

Moral: People often lie to cover up their own mistakes, but honesty is always the best policy.

The Sensible Enemy

In a kingdom, a prince befriended a merchant's son and the son of a man of learning. They spent their days together, enjoying various diversions and pastimes.

The prince often complained to his friends about his father's disapproval of his lack of interest in kingly pursuits like archery and elephant-riding. His friends sympathized with him and said, "We too face similar troubles at home. But now that we see you're also unhappy, we're even more grieved."

The prince decided it was time to leave and find a new life elsewhere. He suggested traveling to Climbing Mountain, where they could find precious gems and satisfy their desires.

The merchant's son agreed, saying, "We need money to achieve our goals. Climbing Mountain is the perfect place to find gems." They set off together.

On Climbing Mountain, each of them discovered a magnificent gem. However, they soon realized they needed to protect their treasures from thieves. The son of the man of learning proposed an unusual plan: they would swallow the gems and carry them in their stomachs.

As they followed this plan, a fellow traveler, who had been watching them, devised a scheme to steal the gems. He joined their group, claiming he needed their protection to reach his home.

The travelers continued their journey, unaware of the danger lurking among them. As they passed through a Bhil village, a bird in a cage began to sing. The village chief, understanding the bird's song, realized they were carrying precious gems.

The chief sent his men to capture the travelers, but they found nothing. The bird sang again, and the chief, convinced of the gems' existence, had the travelers brought back for further inspection.

The chief threatened to cut open their stomachs to find the gems, but the thief had a plan. He knew that if his own stomach was cut open first and nothing was found, the chief would spare the others.

The thief humbly asked the chief to cut his stomach first, and the chief, moved by his words, agreed. However, when the chief examined the thief's stomach, he found no gem.

Realizing his mistake, the chief released the travelers, and they continued their journey. The thief's selfless act saved his friends' lives, and they all reached a safe destination.

Moral: A sensible enemy can be a better friend than a selfish ally.

The Foolish Friend

In a far-off kingdom, a merchant's son had befriended a prince, who made him his secretary of the treasury. Together, they hatched a plan to conquer a neighboring kingdom. The merchant's son was appointed prime minister, and the prince became the king.

As time passed, the king grew lazy and indulged in luxurious pleasures. He made a pet of a mischievous monkey from the palace stables and appointed it his personal sword-bearer. The monkey was spoiled and grew big and strong.

One day, while the king and his queen were taking a stroll in a beautiful pleasure-grove, the monkey was left in charge. A bee buzzed around the king's head, and the monkey, thinking it was a threat, drew its sword and struck the king, killing him.

The queen was shocked and scolded the monkey, saying, "You fool! The king trusted you, and you repaid him with treachery."

The monkey explained what had happened, and the entire court shunned it. The king's death was a tragic reminder that making friends with foolish people can lead to disastrous consequences.

Moral: It's wiser to keep a safe distance from those who lack sense, for they can cause harm to others, just like the monkey killed the king.

The Winning of Friends

In a city called Maidens' Delight, there was a giant banyan tree that sheltered many creatures. A crow named Swift lived in the tree and was known for his quick thinking.

One morning, Swift saw a hunter approaching the tree, armed with a snare and a club. The hunter looked frightening, with bloodshot eyes and a knot of hair on his head. Swift was curious about the hunter's intentions and decided to follow him.

As the hunter set up his snare, Swift warned the other birds to stay away, telling them that the rice-grains were poison. But a dove-king named Gay-Neck, with hundreds of doves, saw the food and ignored Swift's warning. He landed in the snare, and he and his doves were caught.

The hunter was delighted and started to lift his club. But Gay-Neck remained calm and came up with a plan. He told the doves to fly up and work together to carry the snare away. The doves were amazed by Gay-Neck's quick thinking and followed his instructions.

Together, the doves managed to lift the snare and fly away, leaving the hunter frustrated. Swift was impressed by Gay-Neck's leadership and teamwork skills. He realized that when friends work together, they can overcome even the most difficult challenges.

Moral: United action and teamwork can help overcome even the most daunting obstacles.

Self-defeating Forethought

Two hunters were once out in the forest.

Red-Face was hunting a big boar. He saw the boar and drew his bow.

He said, "I will shoot this boar and eat its meat."

Red-Face shot the boar with an arrow. But the boar was very strong.

The boar fought back and hurt Red-Face badly. Both the hunter and the boar died.

A hungry jackal came to the spot. He saw the dead hunter and the dead boar.

The jackal thought, "This is a good luck for me. I will eat and be happy."

The jackal started eating the sinew of the bow. He thought, "I will eat slowly and have food for many days."

But the jackal's greed made him eat too quickly. The bow-tip went into his mouth and hurt him badly.

The jackal died from the pain. Both the hunter and the jackal died because of their own mistakes.

Moral: Greed can be very bad for you.

Mister Duly

There was a merchant named Ocean. He had a son.

The son bought a book for a hundred rupees. The book had one line: "What's duly his, a man receives."

Ocean saw the book and asked his son, "What did you pay for this book?" The son said, "A hundred rupees." Ocean said, "You fool! How can you make money with one line in the book?" He kicked his son out of the house.

The son went to another country. He met people and said, "What's duly his, a man receives." The people called him Mister Duly.

One day, a princess named Moonlight saw a handsome prince. She fell in love with him. She sent her friend to ask the prince to meet her. The prince agreed to meet her.

But the prince thought, "Is it right to go to the princess's house at night?" He read a book and found these lines: "A Brahman-slayer, so they say, / Is he who tries to house / With teacher's child, or wife of friend, / Or royal servant's spouse." He decided not to go.

Mister Duly saw a strap hanging from a house. He climbed up the strap to see what was inside. The princess thought the prince was the one she had sent for. She gave him food, clothes, and a bath. But when the prince spoke, she realized he was not the one she loved. She sent him away.

Mister Duly went to a temple and slept. A policeman came to the temple. Mister Duly said, "What's duly his, a man receives." The policeman said, "This temple is empty. Sleep in my bed."

But Mister Duly lay in the wrong bed. The policeman's daughter, Naughty, woke up and thought Mister Duly was her boyfriend. She married him in the dark. But when she saw him, she scolded him and sent him away.

Mister Duly joined a wedding procession. An elephant came and scared everyone. Mister Duly saved the bride and chased the elephant away.

The king came and asked Mister Duly, "What happened?" Mister Duly said, "What's duly his, a man receives." The king realized that Mister Duly was the one who had saved the princess, the policeman's daughter, and the merchant's daughter.

The king gave Mister Duly his daughter and a thousand villages. He made Mister Duly his crown prince. Mister Duly and his family lived happily ever after.

Moral: What's duly yours, you will receive.

The Mice That Set Elephants Free

There was a big, old village with broken houses.

Mice lived in the cracks of the walls. They were happy.

They had parties, watched plays, and ate yummy food.

But one day, a big elephant king came with his herd.

He crushed some mice with his big feet.

The mice were sad and scared. They had a meeting.

"We must help the elephants," they said.

Some mice went to the elephant king.

"We live near here," they said. "Please don't hurt us."

The elephant king thought about it. He decided to help the mice.

Years later, the elephant king got trapped.

He remembered the mice who helped him.

He sent a message to the mice through an elephant cow.

The mice came to help their friends. They gnawed the ropes.

The elephant king and his herd were free.

Moral: Make friends with everyone, big or small.

Spot's Captivity

There was a deer named Spot. 
He loved to run with his friends. 
One day, he got caught in a hunter's snare. 
The hunter took him home to the prince.

The prince gave Spot nice food and baths. 
He even gave him perfumes and ointments. 
But Spot missed his friends and home. 
He longed to run with them again.

Spot remembered his herd and said: 
"When shall I follow on the herd 
Of coursing deer again? 
When brace myself against the wind 
That whistles by? Ah, when?"

The prince got scared and thought Spot was a magic deer.

In a small village, a carpenter lived with his wife. People in the village spoke ill of her, saying she was unfaithful.

The next day, the carpenter left for the forest, but instead of going far, he hid under the bed in his own house. His wife, thinking she was alone, met her lover and invited him to stay. But as the lover was about to join her in bed, she accidentally stubbed her toe on the carpenter's body.

Thinking it was the carpenter testing her, she came up with a clever plan. She told the lover that a goddess had appeared to her. The goddess said her husband would soon die. If she embraced another man, the death would pass to him. Then her husband would live a hundred years. The lover, believing this, did as she said.

The carpenter, hearing the commotion, emerged from under the bed and accused his wife and the lover of infidelity. But instead of being angry, he praised his wife for being clever and convincing. He even asked the lover to join him in a celebratory dance, claiming that the lover had helped him live longer.

The carpenter's relatives were shocked by his behavior, but he just laughed and said that he was happy to have a long life ahead of him. He danced around the village, with the lover still on his shoulder, much to the amusement of the villagers.

Moral: It's foolish to pardon someone who has clearly done wrong, and even more foolish to reward them for it.

The Cave That Talked

In a dense forest, a hungry lion named Rough-Claw roamed around, searching for food. His throat was parched from thirst and hunger. As the sun began to set, he stumbled upon a massive cave and decided to hide inside.

Presently, the cave's owner, a sly jackal named Curd-Face, arrived at the entrance and started singing, "Cave ahoy! Cave aho-o-oy!" After a brief pause, he continued, "Hello! Don't you remember our agreement? You were supposed to speak to me when I returned, and I would greet you. But today, you're silent. I'll go to that other cave instead."

The lion thought, "This cave usually greets Curd-Face, but today it's quiet because it's afraid of me. I'll call out a greeting, and Curd-Face will follow the sound, providing me with food."

The lion loudly called out a greeting, but the cave's echo amplified the sound, scaring other forest creatures. Curd-Face, meanwhile, escaped, saying, "Joy comes from knowing what to dread, and sorrow strikes the foolish. I've lived in these woods for a long time, but never heard a cave talk."

Curd-Face departed, leaving the lion behind. The lion's plan had backfired.

A wise old owl named Live-Strong was overjoyed at Curd-Face's departure. He thought, "Red-Eye's escape is a blessing for us. He was wise, while the others were foolish. I can easily defeat them now."

Live-Strong started secretly building a woodpile at the fortress gate, planning to set it on fire and destroy the owls. The owls, blinded by their trust, didn't notice Live-Strong's sinister plan.

Cloudy, the king of the forest, was delighted when Live-Strong reported that the enemy's cave was ready to be burned. Cloudy and his followers, each carrying a lighted fagot, flew to the gate and threw the fire on Live-Strong's nest. The owls, trapped inside, could not find their way out of the flames.

Moral: Never trust an enemy, however friendly he seems, and do not make one without cause.

The Monkey and the Crocodile

A great rose-apple tree stood on the shore of the sea, its branches laden with fruit. Red-Face, a mischievous monkey, lived in the tree. One day, a crocodile named Ugly-Mug crawled out of the ocean and burrowed into the soft sand.

Red-Face welcomed the crocodile, offering him rose-apples and saying, "You're my guest, sir. Eat these delicious fruits, and we'll have a lovely conversation." The crocodile enjoyed the rose-apples and the conversation that followed.

When the crocodile returned home, he gave his wife the uneaten rose-apples. She asked him, "Where do you get these nectar fruits?" The crocodile replied, "I have a good friend, a monkey named Red-Face, who gives them to me."

His wife's eyes lit up with desire, and she said, "If you eat these fruits every day, your heart must be turned to nectar. Give me your friend's heart, and I'll eat it. Then I'll never grow old or sick, and I'll be a delightful companion for you."

The crocodile refused, explaining that Red-Face was like a brother to him. He couldn't kill him, especially since he gave them fruit. The crocodile's wife wouldn't give up, accusing him of loving Red-Face and spending all his time with her.

The crocodile was dejected, but he tried to reason with his wife. He said, "When I'm at your feet, why do you look at me with jealousy?" His wife's face swelled with tears, and she scolded him, saying, "You love Red-Face, don't you? His tricks have stolen your heart. My rivalry is futile, sir. Please abstain from this tricky game."

The crocodile visited Red-Face, telling him about his wife's demands. Red-Face was amused and said, "My friend, why have you not been here for so long? Why don't you speak cheerfully and tell a witty joke?" The crocodile explained that his wife wanted Red-Face's heart, but he couldn't kill him.

Red-Face suggested that the crocodile's wife come to the rose-apple tree, but the crocodile said, "My home is on a lovely sand-bank under the water. Climb on my back, and we'll travel comfortably." Red-Face agreed, but as they swam, he became terrified, thinking, "If I fall from his back, I'll drown."

The crocodile thought, "If he falls, he's doomed. I'll tell him my plan, and he can pray to his favorite god." He said, "Sir, I've deceived you, and you'll die because my wife ordered me to do it. Pray to your favorite god." Red-Face asked, "Why did you plan to kill me? What harm have I done your wife or you?"

The crocodile explained that his wife wanted to eat Red-Face's heart because she longed to taste the nectar fruits. Red-Face replied, "If that's the case, why didn't you tell me on shore? I have another heart, very sweet indeed, which I keep in a hole in the rose-apple tree."

The crocodile was delighted and said, "Give me that other heart, and my cross wife will eat it and give up starving herself. I'll take you back to the rose-apple tree." Red-Face laughed and scolded the crocodile, saying, "You fool! You traitor! How can anyone have two hearts? Go home, and never come back under the rose-apple tree."

The crocodile was embarrassed, thinking, "Oh, why was I such a fool as to tell him my plan? If I can win his confidence again, I'll do it." He said, "My friend, she has no need of a heart. What I said was just a joke to test your sentiments. Please come to our house as a guest. Your brother's wife is most eager for you."

Red-Face refused, saying, "Rascal! Go away this moment. I will not come. Tell Handsome, miss, that Theodore will see him in the well no more."

Moral: Those who trust a faithless friend are certain to fall into danger.

Flop-Ear told Dusty that he was mistreated by the laundryman and longed for a better life. Dusty promised him a lovely spot by a river with green grass and three beautiful she-donkeys who would be his companions. Flop-Ear was convinced and followed Dusty to the lion's presence.

Slow, the Weaver

In a town, a weaver named Slow lived. 
He had a loom but all pegs broke.

Slow went to the seashore to find wood. 
There, he saw a big sissoo tree.

A fairy lived in the tree. "Please spare it," the fairy said. 
"My home is here. I'm happy here."

"Why not move?" Slow asked. "I need wood for my loom." 
The fairy said, "Ask me anything, but spare this tree."

Slow went home to ask his friend and wife. 
At home, he met his friend, the barber.

"My friend, the fairy favors me," Slow said. 
"Ask for a kingdom. We'll be king and prime minister."

Slow's wife was not at home. He asked his friend about her. 
The friend said, "Don't ask her. Women give bad advice."

Slow went to his wife. "What to ask the fairy?" he asked. 
She said, "Don't be silly. Ask for a second pair of arms and an extra head."

"I can make two pieces of cloth," Slow thought. 
"I'll be happy and rich."

Slow went back to the fairy. "I want a second pair of arms and an extra head," he said. 
The fairy gave him what he asked for.

But people saw Slow and thought he was a monster. 
They beat him with sticks and stones.

Slow died. The people learned a lesson.

Moral: Ask for what you really need, not what looks nice.

The Brahman's Dream

There lived a Brahman named Seedy in a town.
He begged for barley-meal and got some.
He ate a little and filled a jar with the rest.
He hung the jar on a peg and went to sleep.

Seedy thought, "If famine comes, I'll get 100 rupees from this jar."
He would buy she-goats, and they would have babies.
More goats, cows, buffaloes, and mares would come.
He would sell them and get rich.
He would buy a big house and a lovely daughter.
She would have a son named Moon-Lord.

Seedy imagined himself sitting on the stable roof.
Moon-Lord would jump from his mother's lap to ride on Seedy's knee.
But Seedy would get angry and tell his wife to take the boy.
She would be busy and not listen.

Seedy kicked the jar in his dream.
It broke, and barley-meal spilled all over him.
Seedy turned white from head to toe.

Seedy woke up, and his friends laughed at him.
He looked silly with his white face.

Moral: Don't let your dreams make you forget what's real.

The Credulous Fiend

In a far-off kingdom, King Fine-Army ruled with kindness and wisdom. His daughter, Princess Pearl, was known for her stunning beauty and charming smile. However, a wicked fiend had fallen in love with her and tried to carry her off every evening.

But the princess was clever and protected herself by drawing a magic circle. The fiend couldn't touch her, but he would often scare her with his evil presence. One evening, the princess confided in her friend about the fiend's nightly visits.

The fiend overheard their conversation and thought, "Ah, I'm not the only one after the princess! There's someone else, named Twilight, who also wants to take her away." He decided to disguise himself as a horse and investigate the palace stables to learn more about this rival.

Meanwhile, a horse-thief sneaked into the palace at night, looking for a valuable steed. He spotted the fiend-horse and thought it was the best horse in the stable. As he was about to leave, the fiend, still in horse form, was suddenly struck by the thief with a whip.

The fiend was terrified and started running, but the thief was confused. He thought, "This horse is acting strangely. It's not responding to the bit." The thief realized that the horse must be a fiend in disguise, and he decided to drop from a high spot to save his own life.

As the thief fell, he caught a branch from a banyan tree and stuck there. Both of them were relieved to have found a way to escape the other's clutches.

A mischievous monkey, a friend of the fiend, saw the situation and said, "Why are you running from a harmless man? Eat him!" The fiend transformed back into his true form, but his mind was still troubled. The thief, however, was now angry and took the monkey's tail in his mouth, causing the monkey immense pain.

The fiend, seeing the monkey's distress, tried to reason with him. He said, "You have been caught by Twilight, the one who wins the race. It's time for you to bid me farewell and go home." The monkey, still in agony, couldn't respond and could only wait for his fate to be decided.

Moral: Even the most cunning and powerful can fall prey to their own fears and doubts.

Poor Blossom

Adapted from the Panchatantra

God Indra had a parrot named Blossom. He was incredibly beautiful, intelligent, and well-learned. Blossom loved to sit on Indra's hand, feeling happy and content.

One day, while Blossom was resting on Indra's hand, he saw Yama, the god of death, approaching. Blossom immediately moved away, and the other gods asked him, "Why did you move away, Blossom?" Blossom replied, "Yama brings harm to all living creatures. Why shouldn't I move away from him?"

The gods tried to calm Blossom's fears by asking Yama to spare his life. Yama said, "I don't decide these things. It's Time who decides when someone dies." The gods then took Blossom to meet Time, asking him to spare the parrot's life. But Time said, "It's Death who makes these decisions. Ask him."

The gods asked Yama to speak to Death, and when he did, Blossom died at the mere sight of Death. The gods were shocked and asked Yama, "Why did this happen?" Yama replied, "Blossom's death was simply his fate."

The gods returned to heaven, and the story of Blossom's fate spread throughout the land.

Moral: Sometimes, no matter how hard we try, our fate is already decided.

The Unteachable Monkey

In a forest, a troop of monkeys were shivering with cold one winter evening. They spotted a firefly and thought it was a tiny flame. With great care, they lifted the firefly, covered it with dry grass and leaves, and surrounded themselves with it. They even blew on it, imagining the warmth spreading through their bodies.

The monkey who was the chilliest of all blew repeatedly, his breath hot with excitement. A bird named Needle-Face, who had been watching from a nearby tree, flew down to warn the monkey. "This isn't fire, it's just a firefly!" she cried, but the monkey wouldn't listen.

Needle-Face tried to reason with the monkey, but he just kept blowing, ignoring her warnings. When she shouted right into his ear, he got angry and grabbed her, slamming her against a rock. Unfortunately, the bird's head and neck were badly hurt, and she didn't survive.

The other monkeys were shocked and saddened by the bird's death. They realized that they had been foolish to ignore Needle-Face's warnings. They learned a valuable lesson that day: it's always better to listen to advice from others, rather than stubbornly doing what you think is right.

Moral: Blind stubbornness can lead to great harm, and it's wise to listen to others' advice.
